content: I don't like the name docs#FiniteField.Extension.frob. I get that it's an abbreviation of frobenius, but we spell it in full elsewhere, most notably docs#frobenius.
Just a remark. We have one more gaussSum_frob
I would support a change, I don't like abbreviations like this, but others eg Yael prefer brevity.

I guess one argument for the brevity here is that when mathlib had things like Doset you could quite imagine an expert in algebra saying "what the heck is a doset" which for me was a stong argument to changing it to DoubleCoset, but every number theorist would know that frob=Frobenius. The fact that we have Frobenius elsewhere though makes your case stronger.
@Kevin Buzzard To be fair the infoview and plugin is too strong that one can just “go to definition”.

I'm talking about a mathematician who has no understanding of lean and is trying to figure out what the statement of a theorem says. Because of recent changes in mathematics, more and more of those people are looking at our code.

While being accessible to people inexperienced in Lean is a fine goal, I feel that Lean's infoview is a very powerful mechanism, and it would be somewhat wasteful to optimize for the case of people reading the code without the infoview.

Note. I find it a bit hard to explain what “powerful mechanism” means here, but I'm thinking of:

  • typing code into your own computer and run it immediately is more powerful than writing code on punch card and submit it for batch processing,
  • having a REPL is more powerful than that,
  • having Jupyter notebook is more powerful than that (you can store the code across multiple sessions easily),
  • and I see the infoview being the next step.

It's true that optimizing for the “with infoview” case and the “plaintext” case are not necessarily pulling in opposite directions, but there would be a Pareto frontier, and I doubt it would be a single point. Plus, however nicely you optimize for putting static text in a file, you cannot match the interactivity, which only shows the information the user seeks on demand.

An alternative I can think of is to offer the equivalent of the infoview on all platforms, but this requires having control over GitHub front-end interface (if one wants to display the code on GitHub), and is thus unreasonably difficult. There is Verso, which tries to do “html static rendering” of the interactivity, which I think is better but still fall short of real IDE experience.

(Thought experiment: what if we store all source code in a compressed or encoded format that is _only_ viewable through the IDE or equivalent? Compare with Jupyter notebook or Mathematica notebook (or Microsoft Word document…), nobody wants to read the source code of these)

Digression: I think one cannot figure out what a statement says having no knowledge of Lean anyway: there are quirks of type theory not present in “normal” mathematics.
At the very least, one would likely need to know about variable, instance-implicit parameters, various notation, the A → B → C notation (means A ∧ B → C if they're all propositions), etc.
One may propose “use AI to read back the statement”, but while reasonably accurate for experienced users, I don't think this gives much confidence for those who aren't.

I mean I use the infoview a lot and I still find it helpful to have nice notation and readable names in the syntax. Even if a definition can be looked up in principle, even if just by hovering, having it be more obfuscated still adds cognitive load.

read back the statement

The proper fix is @Kyle Miller and @Patrick Massot's informalization project. A demo already exists, and they are working on making it more ready now. I really look forward to this!

@Artie Khovanov

more obfuscated

I suppose this depends on your perspective. Mathematicians (we) invent new terms all the time as abbreviations of older (sequence of) terms when appropriate.

(On the other hand, if you argue "abbreviating DoubleCoset to Doset is not worth it since both are essentially one mental token", I think that's a reasonable view. But why did we not use Integer for Int? Besides, the line length is 100 characters per line, not say 20 tokens per line.)

(Digression: I think short notation matters more when handwritten than when typed, since it takes more time to write notation by hand than to type them)
Yeah I mean there's obviously a balance to be struck. I think Doset is too far. frob I don't have a strong view on, it's probably fine. I was just objecting to the principle of your view.
We use Z\ZZ for integers so who cares what the type is called (and we can't change it anyway because it's in core)
We have deque for double-ended queue, and nobody complains. I suppose it's just whether the notation has been sufficiently well-established.
On the other hand maybe (? not my area) double coset is relatively uncommon that it's not worth having a shortcut.

deque and int are programming terms, not mathematical ones -- and yes I think that's exactly Artie's "balance" -- whether an abbreviation is acceptable to one person or another is some combination of how much they feel it's standard, how much they are annoyed by the line limit linter and how much they mind typing.
It's one of these things you can bikeshed forever but that ultimately comes down to a pretty arbitrary line
